title: Record: packages, where a package sits, the lock file, the fetch, git and the first-party json
body:
## Design

The owner's answers J-P1 to J-P9 of 2026-11-01 on packages are recorded in `kurz-design.md`, section 13, "Packages". They were given through the question tool on #175:
- J-P1 to J-P6 in comment 6561048414, to the questions of comment 6560746557;
- J-P7 in comment 6562217865, to the question of comment 6561825554;
- J-P8 and J-P9 in comment 6562387367, to the questions of comment 6562284775.

Each comes with what it was chosen against and its cost, as the options named them:

- J-P1 "Cargo's walk": a package is the folder of a git repository that holds its `project.kz`, anywhere in the tree, found by the package's name. A file's `use json` makes the `pub` names of its top folder visible, as C#'s `using` does.
  - It was chosen against Go's form, the repository's root as the package, at the cost of one package per repository or paths in `use`.
  - It was chosen against a fixed `src/`, at the cost of one package per repository and a folder name every package keeps.
  - Its cost: a walk of the fetched tree in the compiler.
- J-P7 "Name first, as Cargo": a line of `project.kz` writes the package's name before its URL, `use json "github.com/kurz-lang/kurz" 1.2`, one form for every line.
  - It was chosen against Go's URL run on to the package's folder, at the cost of finding where the repository ends (a URL form per forge, or a probe) and a URL that changes when the folder moves.
  - It was chosen against the URL alone with a `package` word where it does not end in the name, at the cost of two forms of the line.
  - Its cost: the name on every line, even where the URL ends in it.
  - The sample of section 13 changes with it: `use json "github.com/kurz-lang/kurz" 1.2` and `use mysql "github.com/example/mysql" 0.9 allow network`. The second URL's owner is a neutral `example`, so that the sample names no one. A file's lines `use json` and `use mysql allow network` stay.
- J-P8 "By kind of name": what a file's `use` makes visible goes by the kind of name, for a package and a folder alike.
  - A type is visible unqualified, as C#'s `using` brings types: `Json.Parse<T>(text)`.
  - A function at the top of a folder is reached through the folder's name, as section 2's `sys.Write(...)`. C# reaches every function through its type, and Kurz has functions at the top of a folder.
  - Two folders a file uses that both hold a type of one name are a compile error at the bare use of that name, as C#'s CS0104. The question's example showed that error with the option, so it is part of the answer.
  - It was chosen against Rust's `use` of a module, the folder's name qualifying everything it holds, `json.Json.Parse<T>(text)`, at the cost of a qualifier on every name.
  - It was chosen against every name unqualified, C#'s `using` for functions too, at the cost of section 2's `sys.Write(...)` becoming `Write(...)`.
  - Its cost: two rules, by the kind of name. Section 2's `sys.Write(...)` and J-P1's `Json.Parse<T>(text)` both stand as written.
- J-P9 "One version per repo": every package of a repository takes the repository's version. Its own version line equals the repository's `v` tag, as J-P6 has `json` take the language project's.
  - Packages that need versions of their own split into repositories of their own.
  - It was chosen against a tag for each package, `json-v1.2.0`, read by the caret where it carries the package's name, at the cost of two forms of tag and a rule for which one a package reads.
  - Its cost: the packages of one repository release together. A fix to `yaml` alone tags `v1.2.1` and moves `json` to 1.2.1 as well, as the question's example showed.
- J-P2 "Commit + SHA-256": `project.lock` pins each package's version, the commit and a SHA-256 over the package's files, as Go's `go.sum` and NuGet's `contentHash`. A fetch that gives other files fails.
  - It was chosen against Cargo's commit alone, at the cost of git's SHA-1 as the only hash.
  - It was chosen against the SHA-256 alone, at the cost of the tag read again at each fetch and no record of the commit built.
  - Its cost: a hash over the files at each fetch.
  - The guarantee is written with what it survives, its mechanism and what it does not survive (`knowledge/guarantee-needs-its-mechanism.md`):
    - it survives a rewritten history under a kept commit id, and a forge that serves other bytes;
    - its mechanism is the hash at the fetch;
    - it does not survive a release whose author wrote the harm into it.
- J-P3 "Cargo's: build fetches": a build fetches what the cache lacks. `--offline`, `--locked` and `kurz vendor` stand beside it, and the cache keeps a clone per repository and a checkout per commit.
  - It was chosen against a `kurz fetch` of its own, at the cost of a step before a first build.
  - It was chosen against vendoring always, at the cost of every package's source in the project's history.
  - Its cost: a first build needs the network, and the cache grows until it is cleaned.
- J-P4 "Cargo's caret": `1.2` means `>=1.2.0, <2.0.0` over `v1.2.0` tags, and the lowest tag that satisfies every package is picked. The fetch checks the package's own version line against the tag.
  - It was chosen against Cargo's git keys (`tag`, `branch`, `rev`), at the cost that two tags of one package meet only in the override.
  - It was chosen against a minimum with no upper bound, at the cost of a silent move to a new major.
  - Its cost: a list of the tags, and a check at each fetch.
- J-P5 "System git": the installed `git` executable, as Cargo's `net.git-fetch-with-cli`.
  - It was chosen against a git library inside the command, at the cost of a native library on every platform and credentials it does not read.
  - It was chosen against archives over HTTPS, at the cost of one URL form per forge and a token for a private repository.
  - Its cost: `git` must be installed, with a child process for each fetch.
- J-P6 "Folder of the Kurz repo": `json` is a folder of the language project's repository, versioned by its tags.
  - It was chosen against a repository of its own, at the cost of a second set of gates kept in step by hand.
  - Its cost: a fix to `json` alone needs a tag of the whole repository.

Marked *(assumed)*: the defaults the questions listed, which the owner's answers left standing:
- the package's own `project.kz` names it and its version;
- `project.lock` beside `project.kz`, written by the build, committed, in Kurz's syntax;
- the cache under the `kurz` directory of the user's cache directory (section 2), 0700;
- the tag form `v1.2.0`, and a tag that is no version is ignored.

Marked *(assumed)*, proposed with this record and not put to the owner:
- `git` is looked for in the directories of the path, as clang is (section 2), and run by the full path found there. A bare name handed to Windows' `CreateProcessW` is looked for in the current directory and beside the starting program before the path.
- The rest of Cargo's caret: `1` means `>=1.0.0, <2.0.0`, and `1.2.3` means `>=1.2.3, <2.0.0`. A major of 0 bounds the version by its first number that is not 0, so `0.9` means `>=0.9.0, <0.10.0`. The sample's `mysql` line asks `0.9`.
- The id of J-P8's error, `ambiguous-name`, in the form of `ambiguous-call`.

Section 14, "Open", has no entry on packages left: the two entries the acceptance judgment raised are answered by J-P8 and J-P9.

## Reference and corpus

- `reference/08-functions.md`, F10 "Folders and `use`" (decided, §8, §13): it now says what `use` makes visible by the kind of name, and names the error `ambiguous-name` at the bare use, with the id marked *(assumed)*.
- `reference/12-errors.md`: `ambiguous-name` joins the ids that stand in their rule and not in the table, since it takes two folders and a case is a single file.
- No case changes. A case is a single file with no `project.kz` (chapter 0), so neither a package's fetch nor two used folders can be shown by one. The compiler reads `use` of no folder but the runtime's `sys` (`compiler/README.md`), so no program raises `ambiguous-name`.

## Research findings (node B4)

- Rust 10 (a small standard library, crates for everything, and the supply-chain risk) is met in part. The hash catches a forge that serves other bytes and a rewritten history. It does not catch a release whose author wrote the harm into it, which "Every package on path" and "Index with grants" answer.
- Go 8 (finding trustworthy modules) stays answered by "Index with grants".

No gate, tool, hook, workflow or review rule changes, so neither `knowledge/diagram-gate-map.md` nor `guides/quality-bar.md` applies.

## Checks

- `python3 tools/gates.py` on 0f2dac7, the head pushed, in the image the `gates` job runs in: 8 passed. These were self-tests (1290 cases with 1209 red proofs), tree (882 files), knowledge, reference (231 rules, 655 cases, 0 errors), compiler-tests (3837 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped), unicode-tables, ci-config and push-hook. `merge-checks` FAILs, since the container has no forge login. `pr-title`, `pr-breadth` and `pr-findings` were NOT RUN locally, and run in the `gates` job.
- The same 8 passed on e70a27e, the head the fix after the judgment made (named in the acceptance comment), and the `gates` and `compiler-windows` jobs were green on it.
- The gates were NOT RUN to their end on 8461be0, the head the acceptance judge read: that run was stopped for the fix. The judge did not run again on 0f2dac7, which records the owner's answers to the two questions its failed row raised; the acceptance comment names that commit.
- 03f5e2f merges `main` (0fb2c3c) into the branch, with no conflict. `python3 tools/gates.py` on it, in the same image: the same 8 passed, with self-tests (1290 cases, 1209 red proofs), tree (885 files), reference (231 rules, 655 cases, 64 compile-error ids, 0 errors) and compiler-tests (3880 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped). `merge-checks` FAILED there, as on every run in the container: it cannot log in to the forge. The `pr-*` gates were NOT RUN locally.
- The title check of `tools/pr_gates.py` was run locally on the title, this description and the four commit messages, the merge's among them: no finding.
